input:
Heat exchangers play a vital role in a wide range of industrial processes, and the shell-and-tube design is among the most widely used configurations. This passage reports the performance of a shell-and-tube exchanger that heats propylene glycol as part of a refinery preheat train. The duty of the exchanger was measured at 660 kW. The hot stream entered at 180 °C and left at 130 °C, representing a temperature change of 50 K, while the cold stream entered at 35 °C and left at 55 °C, corresponding to a rise of 20 K. At the two ends of the exchanger, the temperature differences between the streams were 125 K and 95 K respectively, resulting in a log-mean temperature difference of 109.3 K. With an installed area of 54.8 m2, the overall heat transfer coefficient was calculated to be 110 W m-2 K-1.

It is worth noting that fouling was assessed on the basis of a single 90-day run. As no cleaning cycle has yet been completed, the extent to which performance may change over longer periods of operation remains uncertain, and further monitoring will be required in order to fully characterise the long-term behaviour of the exchanger, highlighting the importance of continued data collection.
target:
Duty in the shell-and-tube exchanger is 660 kW, heating propylene glycol in a refinery preheat train. The propylene glycol is the cold stream, heated through the tube walls against the hot stream. The hot stream enters at 180 °C and leaves at 130 °C, a fall of 50 K. The cold stream enters at 35 °C and leaves at 55 °C, a rise of 20 K. The temperature difference between the streams is 125 K at the end where the hot stream enters and 95 K at the end where it leaves, and the log-mean temperature difference is 109.3 K. Installed area is 54.8 m2, and the overall coefficient at the stated conditions is 110 W m-2 K-1.

The coefficient is a single value for the exchanger as tested. It folds the two film resistances and the wall resistance into one number, together with whatever fouling the surfaces carried during the run, and it is separable from the area only as a product: the test fixes the duty, the temperatures, and the area, and the coefficient is what those figures return. Fouling was assessed from a single 90-day run, and no cleaning cycle has been completed. The run therefore states the coefficient for the exchanger in its tested state over the run. How the coefficient moves as fouling builds across a longer campaign, and what cleaning restores, are both outside the record, and a figure carried into design for a longer run needs a fouling allowance this test does not supply.
